gloss_terse: gashes, cuts (on the body as expression of mourning)
gloss_readable: This rare term appears only in Jeremiah's oracle against Moab, describing ritual self-mutilation as a sign of grief. The Hebrew root relates to cutting or incising, and the context at Jeremiah 48:37 places it alongside shaved heads and clipped beards—all forbidden mourning practices in Israel but common among surrounding nations. The English 'gashes' and Spanish 'cortaduras' capture the visceral physicality of this ancient grief expression.

senses.1: Referring to deliberate cuts made on the body during mourning rituals, this sense is attested only in Jeremiah 48:37 where it describes pagan Moabite grief practices. The multilingual evidence (English 'gashes', Spanish 'cortaduras') confirms the physical violence of the act, contrasting with Israel's covenant prohibitions against such bodily mutilation in mourning contexts.

gloss_readable: Found only in Psalm 65:10, this agricultural term describes the corrugated surface of plowed land. The psalm celebrates God's provision through rain that softens the ridges and furrows, making the earth fruitful. While the Hebrew root relates to cutting or trenching, here it evokes the parallel grooves created by the plow. The imagery connects divine blessing with the practical realities of ancient Near Eastern farming.

senses.1: The ridged terrain created by plowing, appearing in Psalm 65:10's hymn of agricultural thanksgiving. God's rain 'settles its ridges' (English, German) or 'terrones' (Spanish clods/furrows), softening the hardened ground. The French 'incision' highlights the cutting action that creates these furrows, essential for seed planting and water retention.

gloss_readable: This lone occurrence in Proverbs 19:19 appears in a challenging textual context. The verse discusses someone 'great of wrath' or 'prone to great anger,' warning that rescuing such a person repeatedly only perpetuates their destructive patterns. The adjective conveys magnitude and intensity, whether physical size, emotional force, or social significance. Though monosemous here, it participates in the broader semantic field of Hebrew words for greatness.

senses.1: Used adjectivally to intensify 'wrath' in Proverbs 19:19, describing someone characterized by great or excessive anger. All four languages (English 'great', Spanish 'grande', French 'grand', German participle form) preserve this sense of magnitude, here applied to temperamental intensity rather than physical size.

gloss_terse: Haggedolim (proper name: 'the great ones' or personal name)
gloss_readable: This enigmatic form in Nehemiah 11:14 has sparked debate among translators and textual critics. The Revised Version and most modern scholars read it as a personal name (Haggedolim, father of Zabdiel), while the Greek Septuagint and RV margin interpret it as 'the great ones' or 'the nobles'—a title rather than a name. The definite article and plural form support the titular reading, yet genealogical lists typically require proper names. This ambiguity reflects the challenges of post-exilic Hebrew onomastics.

senses.1: Either the proper name of Zabdiel's father or a title meaning 'the great ones/nobles' in Nehemiah 11:14. The English and BDB lean toward the personal name interpretation, while Greek witnesses favor the titular sense. Spanish simply transliterates 'S' (possibly an abbreviation), and French/German preserve the Hebrew form, acknowledging the textual uncertainty.

gloss_readable: Appearing only in Ezekiel 5:15, this term belongs to a cluster of humiliation vocabulary. God warns that Jerusalem will become 'a reproach and a taunt, an admonition and an astonishment' to surrounding nations after judgment falls. The word conveys not mere criticism but scornful derision—the kind of mocking insult enemies heap upon the defeated. BDB notes the unique occurrence and the parallel structure linking multiple shame terms, each intensifying the portrait of national disgrace.

senses.1: A scornful taunt or mocking reproach in Ezekiel 5:15, where Jerusalem's downfall becomes an object lesson for nations. English 'taunt' and Spanish 'escarnio' (mockery) capture the derisive quality, while French 'reproche' emphasizes the reproachful aspect. The term appears in a foursome with 'reproach, admonition, astonishment,' creating a comprehensive picture of covenant judgment.

gloss_readable: One of the twelve spies sent to scout Canaan in Numbers 13, Gaddi represented the tribe of Manasseh. His name derives from the Hebrew root for fortune or luck, perhaps reflecting parental gratitude at his birth or hopes for his future. BDB notes the theophoric-like structure ('my fortune') common in ancient Semitic naming. He remains otherwise unknown in biblical narrative beyond this single genealogical reference, one among the ten unfaithful spies whose negative report led to Israel's forty-year wilderness wandering.

senses.1: The personal name of Manasseh's representative among the twelve spies (Numbers 13:11), meaning 'my fortune' or 'my luck.' All four languages preserve the proper name unchanged (Gaddi/Gadi/Gaddi), following standard transliteration practice for biblical personal names. The theological irony is that despite his name meaning 'fortunate,' he was among the majority who brought a faithless report.

gloss_readable: Another of the twelve spies sent to Canaan, Gaddiel represented Zebulun according to Numbers 13:10. His name combines the fortune/luck root with the divine name El, creating a theophoric confession: 'God is my fortune.' This naming pattern—attributing good fortune to deity rather than chance—reflects typical Israelite theology. Like Gaddi of Manasseh, Gaddiel appears only in the spy list and presumably joined the faithless majority, making his name's theological claim ironic in light of his subsequent unbelief.

senses.1: The name of Zebulun's spy representative (Numbers 13:10), meaning 'El is my fortune' or 'God is my luck.' The theophoric element 'El' elevates mere fortune language to theological confession. All languages preserve the proper name through transliteration (Gaddiel/Gadiel), standard practice for biblical personal names, though Spanish slightly varies the spelling.

gloss_readable: This feminine plural form appears only in Song of Songs 1:8, where the beloved is directed to pasture her young goats beside the shepherds' tents. The pastoral imagery evokes the countryside courtship setting common in ancient Near Eastern love poetry. The word specifically denotes young female goats (kids), distinguished from mature animals and from male kids. The possessive suffix ('your kids') emphasizes the beloved's role as shepherdess, a romantic idealization of rural life that pervades the Song.

senses.1: Young female goats belonging to the beloved shepherdess in Song of Songs 1:8. The multilingual evidence is consistent: English 'young goats', Spanish 'cabritas' (little she-goats), French 'chevreaux' (kids), all emphasizing the youth and pastoral charm of these animals. The parallel with 'the flock' confirms the agricultural setting of this love poem.

gloss_readable: Job 21:32 presents a rare and contested word. BDB identifies it as a tomb or burial mound, citing Arabic cognates for 'grave.' The context supports this: even the wicked man 'is borne to the grave' and receives honorable burial. However, Driver suggested emending to a more common Hebrew word for 'heap.' The Arabic parallel strengthens the tomb reading, as ancient Near Eastern burials often involved mounded earth over the deceased. This hapax legomenon illustrates how Job's archaic vocabulary sometimes preserves rare Semitic roots.

senses.1: Most likely a tomb or burial mound in Job 21:32, though textual uncertainty remains. The Arabic cognate جَدَثٌ 'tomb' supports BDB's reading. English translates generically as 'heap,' Spanish 'montón' likewise, while French and German preserve the Hebrew form, acknowledging the lexical difficulty. The context of burial and watch-keeping over the grave favors the sepulchral interpretation.

gloss_readable: This location appears only in Judges 20:45 during the civil war between Benjamin and the other tribes. Gidom marked the eastern limit of Israel's pursuit of fleeing Benjamites—a tragic boundary in Israel's bloodiest internal conflict. The name may derive from roots meaning 'cutting' or 'severing,' grimly appropriate for a battle site. The place remains unidentified archaeologically, though its position along the wilderness road from Gibeah suggests a location east of Benjamin's territory.

senses.1: A geographical marker in Benjamin's territory (Judges 20:45) where Israel's pursuit of Benjamin ended. All languages transliterate the proper name (Gidom/Guidom), standard for unidentified biblical place names. The military context—a pursuit ending point—may inform the name's meaning, though etymology remains uncertain. This single reference reflects the historical specificity of Judges' civil war narrative.

gloss_readable: Listed among Joshua's thirty-one defeated Canaanite kings in Joshua 12:13, Geder represents one of many small city-states that controlled pre-conquest Canaan. Its location remains debated, though some scholars connect it with Beth-geder in 1 Chronicles 2:51 or with the gentilicadjective 'Gederite' found elsewhere. The Greek Septuagint renders it Gader, and Eusebius mentions it in his Onomasticon, suggesting it was known in later periods. The name likely derives from roots meaning 'wall' or 'enclosure,' common for fortified settlements.

senses.1: A Canaanite city-state conquered during Joshua's southern campaign (Joshua 12:13), location uncertain but possibly in Judah's Shephelah region. All translations preserve the proper name through transliteration (Geder), following standard geographic naming conventions. The conquest list context emphasizes Israel's comprehensive defeat of Canaanite political structures rather than providing detailed geographical information.

gloss_readable: This settlement appears with the definite article in Joshua 15:36 as 'the Gederah,' suggesting it was a well-known place in Judah's lowland district. The town list context groups it with other Shephelah cities in the western foothills between the mountains and coastal plain. Some Greek manuscripts question its inclusion, noting numerical discrepancies in the list, but Hebrew tradition maintains it. The name derives from 'wall' or 'sheepfold,' indicating either fortification or pastoral economy. It may be the same place mentioned in connection with David's mighty men and Hezekiah's porters.

senses.1: A town in Judah's Shephelah region (Joshua 15:36), appearing with the conjunction 'and-the-Gederah' in the territorial list. Spanish 'Gederá' and French 'Gederah' preserve the proper name, while English and German include the definite article, reflecting the Hebrew form. The Shephelah context suggests a fortified settlement in the agricultural lowlands between mountain and coast.

gloss_readable: This ethnic or geographical designation appears in 1 Chronicles 27:28, identifying an official in David's administration. The gentilicial form indicates origin from the city Geder (see H1445), though scholars debate whether it refers to that conquest-list city or to Gederah in Judah. The Greek Septuagint readings (Gedoreiths, Geddoriths) reflect uncertainty about the underlying place name. Such geographical identifiers were common in administrative lists, helping distinguish individuals with identical personal names—essential in royal bureaucracies.

senses.1: A gentilicial designation meaning 'one from Geder' in 1 Chronicles 27:28, identifying a Davidic official. English 'the Gederite' and Spanish 'el gederita' follow standard patterns for forming ethnic/geographical adjectives. French and German preserve the Hebrew form, perhaps acknowledging the textual uncertainty about which 'Geder' is meant. The administrative context requires specific geographical identification.

gloss_readable: Another geographical identifier, this one appearing in 1 Chronicles 12:4 (English 12:5), where it designates one of David's early supporters at Ziklag. The form derives from Gederah rather than Geder, distinguished by an additional syllable. These Ziklag warriors joined David when he was still a fugitive from Saul, representing cross-tribal support that presaged his eventual kingship. The gentilicial precision in Chronicles reflects that work's interest in genealogical and geographical accuracy, preserving clan and regional identities even centuries after the events.

senses.1: Meaning 'one from Gederah,' this designation appears in 1 Chronicles 12:5 identifying one of David's early warriors. English 'the Gederathite' and Spanish 'el guederatita' use standard gentilicial forms, while French and German preserve the Hebrew, acknowledging the specialized nature of such adjectives. The Ziklag context emphasizes the geographical diversity of David's initial coalition.

gloss_readable: This peculiar dual-form place name appears in the same Joshua 15:36 list as Gederah, immediately following it. The dual ending suggests either two settlements bearing the Gederah name or a single place characterized by paired features (two sheepfolds, two walls). The Greek Septuagint omits it, and some modern scholars propose deleting it to resolve the verse's numerical problems (the total count exceeds the stated number). If original, it represents the dual morphology occasionally found in Hebrew place names, often indicating paired geographical features.

senses.1: A place name in Judah's Shephelah (Joshua 15:36), possibly meaning 'two Gederoths' or 'double enclosure.' All languages transliterate the proper name (Gederotayim/Gederotaim), though Greek manuscript tradition questioned its originality. The dual form is morphologically interesting but semantically uncertain—it might indicate twin settlements, paired sheepfolds, or simply a variant spelling. Textual critics debate its authenticity.

gloss_terse: textual error for 'this' (זֶה misread as גֵּה)
gloss_readable: Ezekiel 47:13 contains what virtually all scholars recognize as a scribal error. The received Hebrew text reads an otherwise unknown word (geh), but ancient versions and all modern translations correct it to zeh ('this'), which makes perfect sense in context: 'This is the boundary by which you shall divide the land.' The confusion likely arose from visual similarity between the Hebrew letters zayin and gimel in certain script styles. Such textual corrections, supported by unanimous versional evidence, demonstrate the value of comparative text criticism.

senses.1: A scribal error in Ezekiel 47:13 where the Hebrew consonants were misread. The correct reading is זֶה 'this,' supported by Greek Septuagint, Targum, Vulgate, and all modern scholars. English 'this' and Spanish 'este' represent the corrected text, while French 'erreur' explicitly labels it an error. BDB's entry exists solely to guide readers away from the mistaken form toward the correct reading.

gloss_terse: to heal, cure, be cured (of wounds)
gloss_readable: This rare verb appears only in Hosea 5:13, where it describes the failure of political solutions to heal Judah's 'wound.' The root conveys being freed from pain or disease, with Aramaic cognates supporting the healing sense. Hosea's metaphor is pointed: just as physical wounds require proper treatment, so Israel's spiritual-political crisis cannot be cured by Assyrian intervention. The negative context ('will not cure') emphasizes the futility of trusting foreign powers rather than returning to Yahweh, the true healer.

senses.1: To cure or heal a wound, used metaphorically in Hosea 5:13 for political healing. The prophet declares that foreign alliances 'will not cure' Israel's malady. English 'cure,' Spanish 'curará,' and French 'guérir' all employ standard medical vocabulary, confirming the therapeutic sense. The Aramaic cognate background (ܓܗܳܐ 'be freed from disease') supports BDB's semantic analysis of deliverance from affliction.

gloss_readable: Found only in Proverbs 17:22, this noun appears in one of wisdom literature's most memorable health proverbs: 'A joyful heart makes for good healing' (or 'is good medicine'). The saying contrasts emotional states' physical effects—joy promotes healing while depression harms the bones. The word derives from the verbal root meaning to cure or be freed from disease, here nominalized to express the healing process or its result. This psychosomatic wisdom anticipates modern understanding of emotional health's impact on physical wellbeing.

senses.1: Healing or cure in Proverbs 17:22's wisdom saying about joy's therapeutic power. English 'healing,' Spanish 'medicina' (medicine), and German 'Heilung' (healing) all capture the medical/therapeutic sphere. French preserves the Hebrew form, perhaps acknowledging its rarity. The context links emotional disposition (joyful heart) to physical health outcomes, a sophisticated insight for ancient wisdom literature.

gloss_readable: Job 30:5 employs this Aramaic-influenced noun in describing social outcasts: 'from the midst they are driven.' The word represents an Aramaism in biblical Hebrew, sharing forms with Aramaic, Syriac, and Arabic terms for 'middle' or 'interior.' Some translations render it 'community' or 'society,' emphasizing social rather than spatial position. Job's archaic language frequently preserves such rare or borrowed terms, contributing to the book's linguistic distinctiveness. The phrase echoes Cicero's Latin expression 'driven from the midst,' suggesting a common ancient metaphor for social expulsion.

senses.1: The midst or interior, here meaning the community of people in Job 30:5. The outcasts are 'driven from the midst (of society).' English 'midst,' Spanish 'comunidad' (community), and French 'corps' (body/group) variously interpret whether the term is spatial or social. The Aramaic background (ܓܰܘ 'middle, interior, belly') confirms the root meaning, though context determines whether it's physical space or social sphere.

gloss_readable: The Ketiv (written text) of 2 Kings 25:12 contains a participial form meaning 'diggers' or 'ploughmen,' referring to agricultural workers left in the land after the Babylonian deportation. However, the Qere (reading tradition) and the parallel passage in Jeremiah 52:16 have a different form. The Arabic cognate (جَابَ 'pierce, bore, hollow out') supports the digging/plowing sense. This textual variation illustrates how the Masoretes preserved both written and oral traditions even when they diverged, leaving final decisions to readers and translators.

senses.1: Agricultural workers, diggers or ploughmen, in 2 Kings 25:12's account of the poor left in Judah. The multilingual glosses 'farmers' (English, Spanish, French, German) reflect the occupational sense rather than translating the verbal root directly. The context contrasts these agricultural laborers with the skilled workers and elites deported to Babylon, emphasizing that Nebuchadnezzar left only the poorest to work the land.

gloss_readable: Nahum 3:17 employs this rare locust term in describing the multitude of Assyrian officials: 'like a swarm of locusts.' Hebrew has multiple words for locusts and grasshoppers, each perhaps denoting different species or life stages. This particular term emphasizes the swarming behavior—the massive numbers that characterize locust plagues. The comparison to Assyria's bureaucrats is apt: numerous, consuming, and ultimately transient. When the sun rises, they flee, leaving nothing behind—a prophecy of Nineveh's sudden collapse.

senses.1: A swarm of locusts in Nahum 3:17, used metaphorically for Assyrian officials. English 'swarm of' and Spanish 'enjambre de' (swarm of) emphasize the collective noun aspect, while French 'sauterelle' (locust/grasshopper) focuses on the species. The comparison exploits locusts' characteristic behavior: vast numbers, voracious consumption, and sudden disappearance when conditions change—all apt for describing a doomed empire's administration.

gloss_readable: Job 20:25 presents a contested anatomical term. The verse describes an arrow being extracted 'from the back,' completing the image of a fleeing warrior struck from behind. However, ancient versions (Septuagint, Thes, De) understood it as 'body' more generally. Hoffmann proposed a slight textual emendation. The root meaning involves the external surface or back side of the torso. This lexical ambiguity reflects ancient anatomical vocabulary's lack of the precision modern medicine requires. Context—a weapon's extraction—clarifies that it's the arrow's exit point from the body.

senses.1: The back or external surface of the body in Job 20:25, from which a struck arrow is extracted. English 'body' and Spanish 'cuerpo' (body) interpret broadly, while French and German preserve the Hebrew consonants, acknowledging lexical difficulty. The military context (fleeing, struck, arrow withdrawn) suggests the back specifically, as warriors struck while running would be hit from behind. Ancient versions vary between 'back' and general 'body.'

gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun appears in Daniel 4:37 (4:34 in BDB's Aramaic numbering) in Nebuchadnezzar's climactic confession. After his humbling period of madness, the king acknowledges that God 'is able to humble those who walk in pride.' The Aramaic form corresponds to Hebrew ge'ah (pride, arrogance), showing the regular dialect relationship. The context makes pride's negative quality explicit: it provokes divine humiliation. Nebuchadnezzar's testimony becomes biblical literature's most dramatic example of pride preceding a fall—and subsequent repentance.

senses.1: Arrogant pride in Daniel 4:37, the spiritual disease Nebuchadnezzar confesses after his humiliation and restoration. English 'pride,' Spanish 'soberbia' (arrogance/pride), and the prepositional phrase 'in pride' all capture the moral negativity. French 'exil' (exile) may reflect a different textual understanding or translation tradition. The theological point is clear: God opposes the proud and humbles those who walk in self-exaltation.

gloss_readable: Ecclesiastes 10:8 uses this Aramaic loanword in a proverb about work's inherent dangers: 'He who digs a pit may fall into it.' The saying warns that schemes intended to trap others can ensnare the schemer. The word appears again in Proverbs 26:27 in the Targum and Peshitta, though the Hebrew text there uses a different term. As an Aramaic borrowing in late biblical Hebrew, it illustrates the linguistic influence of Imperial Aramaic on post-exilic Hebrew. The wisdom tradition favored such proverbial warnings about poetic justice.

senses.1: A pit dug in the ground, appearing in Ecclesiastes 10:8's wisdom saying about schemes backfiring. English 'pit,' Spanish 'hoyo' (hole/pit), all identify the excavated trap. French and German preserve the Hebrew form, acknowledging the word's rarity and Aramaic origin. The proverbial context emphasizes ironic reversal: the pit-digger becomes the pit's victim, a common wisdom motif about justice and consequence.

gloss_readable: This gentilicial adjective appears in Numbers 26:48, designating descendants of Guni in the tribal census. The form follows standard Hebrew patterns for creating clan designations from personal names. However, textual critics propose reading the same gentilicial in two disputed passages: 2 Samuel 23:32 and 1 Chronicles 11:34, where the received text has different forms. The Septuagint readings in those passages support the emendation. Such textual proposals illustrate how gentilicial forms, being relatively uncommon, were susceptible to scribal confusion.

senses.1: A clan designation meaning 'descendants of Guni' in Numbers 26:48's census list. English 'the Gunite,' Spanish 'los gunitas' (plural), French 'le Gunite,' and German 'der Gunite' all follow standard gentilicial translation patterns. The definite article with collective noun can be rendered singular ('the Gunite [clan]') or plural ('the Gunites'). The census context requires precise clan identification for territorial allotment purposes.

gloss_readable: This verb appears only in Nehemiah 7:3 in the Hiphil stem, where Nehemiah issues security instructions: 'Let them shut the doors and bar them.' The command reflects post-exilic Jerusalem's vulnerability—even with rebuilt walls, the city required vigilant gate management. The verbal root, occurring only this once in biblical Hebrew, has parallels in later rabbinic Hebrew where it commonly means 'shut' or 'close.' The context of urban security and nightly gate-closing illustrates the practical challenges of maintaining a defended city with a sparse population.

senses.1: To close or shut doors, specifically in Nehemiah 7:3's security protocol for Jerusalem's gates. English 'shut,' Spanish 'cerrarán' (they will close), confirm the action. French and German preserve the Hebrew form, perhaps due to the verb's rarity. The jussive mood ('let them shut') indicates Nehemiah's administrative command, part of his systematic approach to Jerusalem's restoration and security.

gloss_readable: This location appears in 2 Kings 9:27 during Jehu's violent purge of Ahab's house. King Ahaziah of Judah was struck 'at the ascent of Gur, which is by Ibleam' while fleeing Jehu's coup. The site remains archaeologically unidentified, though the reference to an 'ascent' suggests hilly terrain. The name may derive from the root meaning 'to sojourn' or 'dwell,' possibly indicating a caravanserai or way-station. The geographical precision in Kings' narrative reflects the historical particularity of this violent episode.

senses.1: A place near Ibleam where Ahaziah was mortally wounded (2 Kings 9:27). All languages preserve the proper name through transliteration (Gur), standard for unidentified biblical locations. The qualifying phrase 'ascent of Gur' indicates elevated terrain along the road from Jezreel to Samaria. Though location remains uncertain, the narrative specificity serves to anchor this pivotal moment in Israel's dynastic history.

gloss_readable: Found only in 2 Chronicles 26:7, this place name identifies where certain Arabs dwelt whom God helped Uzziah defeat. The compound name combines 'dwelling' with the deity name Baal, suggesting either a Canaanite religious site or simply a place where Baal was worshiped. The location remains unknown, though the context of Arabian inhabitants suggests Judah's southern or eastern frontier. Such compound names combining geographical terms with deity names were common in the ancient Near East, marking sacred sites or territories associated with particular gods.

senses.1: A location associated with Arabian inhabitants in 2 Chronicles 26:7, meaning 'dwelling of Baal.' All languages transliterate the compound proper name (Gur-Baal/Gur-Baal), sometimes preserving the prepositional prefix ('in Gur-Baal'). The Baal element indicates either Canaanite religious influence among these Arabs or simply a place-name incorporating the common Semitic term for 'lord.' Uzziah's campaign context suggests frontier territory beyond Judah's core.

gloss_readable: This Persian administrative title appears in Ezra 1:8, where Cyrus commands 'Mithredath the treasurer' to inventory and release the temple vessels. The word entered Hebrew as a loanword during the Persian period, reflecting the administrative terminology of the Achaemenid Empire. Similar forms appear in Aramaic and Syriac. The Persian original relates to treasure-keeping, an essential function in ancient bureaucracies where wealth was stored physically rather than electronically. Such loanwords in Ezra-Nehemiah authenticate those books' Persian-period setting.

senses.1: A treasury official in the Persian administration (Ezra 1:8), responsible for managing royal or temple wealth. English 'treasurer' and Spanish 'tesorero' use cognate Romance terms, while French and German preserve the Hebrew/Persian form, acknowledging its loanword status. The definite article ('the treasurer') may indicate this was Mithredath's official title rather than a generic description. The context of releasing temple vessels confirms the treasury management role.

gloss_readable: The Aramaic plural of the Persian loanword for 'treasurer' appears in Ezra 7:21, where Artaxerxes commands 'all the treasurers in the province Beyond the River' to supply Ezra's needs. The emphatic plural ending marks this as Biblical Aramaic rather than Hebrew. The Persian administrative context is crucial: multiple regional treasurers managed the vast empire's finances across satrapies. This verse illustrates the Persian government's support for Ezra's mission, providing official backing and financial resources for Jerusalem's temple and Torah community.

senses.1: Regional treasury officials in the Persian administration (Ezra 7:21), plural form commanding multiple treasurers across Trans-Euphrates province. English 'treasurers' and Spanish 'tesoreros' render the plural, while French and German preserve the Aramaic form with its distinctive emphatic plural ending. The administrative context shows the Persian system's bureaucratic sophistication, with specialized financial officers throughout the provinces answerable to royal directives.

gloss_readable: Psalm 71:6 contains a rare verb whose meaning remains disputed. The psalmist declares, 'You are the one who severed me from my mother's womb'—or perhaps 'you are my benefactor.' The Septuagint read 'protector,' while others propose 'the one who drew me out,' connecting to birth imagery. The parallel in Psalm 22:10 uses a clearer verb for being brought from the womb. Textual critics like Cheyne and Duhm have proposed various emendations. This lexical ambiguity doesn't obscure the essential point: God's care from conception onward.

senses.1: To sever or cut from the womb, possibly meaning 'deliver' in Psalm 71:6. English 'cut me' and Spanish 'el que me sacó' (the one who brought me out) interpret toward birth/delivery. French 'mesurer' (measure) and German's long compound suggest alternative understandings. The root may relate to Talmudic Aramaic גְּזָא 'cut off' or to Arabic 'requite,' showing the interpretive range. Despite lexical uncertainty, the verse's theology is clear: divine care from birth.

gloss_readable: First Chronicles 11:34 contains what most scholars recognize as a textual corruption: 'Hashem the Gizonite.' The Septuagint Lucianic recension reads 'Jashen the Gunite,' which aligns with the parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:32. The consonantal similarity between Hebrew letters allowed the error to occur in transmission. BDB cross-references to 'Gunite,' indicating the probable original reading. Such textual corrections, supported by parallel passages and versional evidence, demonstrate how comparative text criticism resolves scribal errors while preserving the received text tradition.

senses.1: A corrupted gentilicial in 1 Chronicles 11:34, likely an error for 'the Gunite' based on Greek Septuagint evidence and the parallel 2 Samuel passage. English 'the Gizonite' and Spanish 'el gizoní' preserve the Masoretic reading, while French and German acknowledge the Hebrew form. The textual problem illustrates how genealogical lists, with their many proper names and gentilicials, were especially susceptible to scribal confusion during transmission.

gloss_readable: Leviticus 16:22 uses this noun to describe where the scapegoat is sent: 'to a land of separation.' The term derives from roots meaning to cut or divide, here indicating a remote, isolated place from which the goat would not return. Some translations render it 'solitary land' or 'cut-off place,' emphasizing the geographical isolation. The ritual's theology is profound: the goat bearing Israel's sins is sent away permanently, symbolizing complete removal of guilt. The land's very name ('separation') underscores the irreversibility of this symbolic act.

senses.1: A remote, separated land where the scapegoat is released (Leviticus 16:22), never to return. English 'cutting-off,' Spanish 'separación' (separation), and French/German cognates all emphasize the isolation. The root meaning of severing or dividing creates the sense of a place definitively cut off from inhabited areas. The ritual context gives theological significance: just as the land is separated from civilization, so Israel's sins are separated from the people.

gloss_readable: This name appears in Genesis 22:24 among the sons born to Nahor (Abraham's brother) by his concubine Reumah. The suggested etymology 'flame' connects to roots for burning or heat, though ancient names' meanings often remain conjectural. As Abraham's nephew, Gaham represents one of the Aramean peoples related to but distinct from Israel. The genealogical notice establishes kinship connections between Israel and surrounding peoples, a recurring interest in Genesis. Gaham himself plays no further role in biblical narrative beyond this genealogical reference.

senses.1: A son of Nahor and Reumah in Genesis 22:24, possibly meaning 'flame' or 'burning.' All languages preserve the proper name through transliteration (Gaham/Gacham), following standard conventions for biblical personal names. The genealogical context links Abraham's family to Aramean peoples northeast of Canaan. The name's etymology remains uncertain, though theophoric-free names in Genesis often derive from natural phenomena or characteristics.

gloss_readable: Daniel 7:2 employs a feminine plural participle describing the four winds of heaven 'stirring up' the great sea, from which emerge the four symbolic beasts. The image evokes chaos and divine providence working through natural and supernatural forces. The verb conveys violent agitation—not gentle rippling but storm-force churning that brings forth the apocalyptic visions. This rare participial form contributes to Daniel's distinctive Aramaic vocabulary, part of the book's heavenly throne-room and cosmic conflict imagery.

senses.1: The violent stirring or churning of the sea in Daniel 7:2, caused by the four winds that precede the apocalyptic beast visions. English 'stirring up,' Spanish 'agitando' (agitating), capture the tumultuous action. French 'poitrine' (chest/breast) appears anomalous, possibly a translation error or variant reading. The imagery evokes primordial chaos, from which symbolic world empires emerge—a fitting apocalyptic metaphor for history's turbulent flow under divine sovereignty.

gloss_readable: This location appears in 2 Samuel 2:24 during the pursuit following the battle between David's and Ish-bosheth's forces. Joab and Abishai pursued Abner 'as far as the hill of Ammah which is before Giah, on the way to the wilderness of Gibeon.' The name may derive from roots meaning 'gush forth' or 'spring,' suggesting a water source. The site remains unidentified archaeologically, but the narrative's geographical precision serves to anchor this episode in the civil war that followed Saul's death.

senses.1: A geographical marker near Gibeon in Benjamin (2 Samuel 2:24), possibly named for a spring or water source. All languages preserve the proper name through transliteration (Giah/Giaj), standard for unidentified biblical sites. The context—a boundary in Joab's pursuit of Abner—provides relative location (before Giah, toward Gibeon's wilderness) without enabling modern identification. The name contributes to the narrative's historical particularity.

gloss_readable: Daniel 1:10 contains an Aramaic noun meaning age or generation: 'the youths who are of your age.' The term relates to Arabic jīl and Samaritan Hebrew for 'generation,' and to the Talmudic phrase 'contemporary' (literally 'son of his age'). The semantic development from 'circle' to 'generation' to 'age cohort' reflects ancient Near Eastern cyclical concepts of time. This Aramaism in Daniel reflects the linguistic milieu of the Babylonian court, where multiple languages and dialects intersected.

senses.1: Age or generation in Daniel 1:10, specifically the age cohort of the youths with Daniel. English 'your age,' Spanish 'vuestra edad' (your age), and French 'vague' (wave/generation) all attempt to render the temporal comparison. German preserves the Hebrew form. The context requires identifying peers of comparable age for the king's dietary comparison. The Arabic and Talmudic cognates confirm the generation/age-cohort meaning.

gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun appears in Daniel 5:5 during Belshazzar's feast: the divine hand wrote on 'the plaster of the wall.' The word denotes chalk, lime, or plaster—the white coating applied to palace walls in ancient Mesopotamia. The Targum confirms this meaning, which persists in later Jewish Aramaic. The detail enhances the scene's dramatic visual: dark letters appearing on white plaster, visible to the terrified king and court. The writing surface itself becomes part of the supernatural sign's impact.

senses.1: The plastered or whitewashed surface of Belshazzar's palace wall in Daniel 5:5, where the mysterious hand writes the judgment oracle. English 'plaster,' Spanish 'yeso' (plaster/gypsum), and French 'chaux' (lime/chalk) all identify the lime-based coating common in ancient Near Eastern architecture. German preserves the Aramaic form. The white surface provided ideal contrast for the divine writing to appear clearly, adding to the sign's terrifying visibility.

gloss_readable: This name appears in 1 Chronicles 2:47 among Caleb's descendants through Judah's lineage. The Chronicles genealogies trace multiple branches of Judah's tribal family, establishing territorial and clan relationships. Geshan represents one minor figure in this extensive genealogical network. The name's etymology remains uncertain, though it may relate to roots for feeling or touching. Like many genealogical names in Chronicles, Geshan serves primarily to establish family connections rather than to mark an individual with narrative significance.

senses.1: A descendant of Judah through Caleb's line in 1 Chronicles 2:47. All languages preserve the proper name through transliteration (Geshan/Gueisan), with French and German maintaining the Hebrew form including the conjunction. The genealogical context serves Chronicles' interest in establishing Judah's clans and their relationships, though Geshan himself receives no further mention in Scripture. The name contributes to the comprehensive family archive.

gloss_terse: barbers (those who cut hair and beards)
gloss_readable: Ezekiel 5:1 contains the only biblical occurrence of this occupational term. The prophet receives a bizarre sign-act command: 'Take a barber's razor and pass it over your head and beard.' The word derives from roots meaning to shave or cut, here nominalized to designate the profession. Phoenician inscriptions confirm the term's wider Semitic usage. The symbolism is profound: Jerusalem's inhabitants will be 'shaved'—removed through death, exile, and dispersion. The barber's tool becomes an instrument of divine judgment rather than routine grooming.

senses.1: The occupational designation 'barbers' in Ezekiel 5:1, those who professionally cut hair and shave beards. English, Spanish, and French all use their respective words for 'barber' (barberos, barbier), while German preserves the Hebrew plural form. The context—'a barber's razor'—makes the professional tool metaphorical for Jerusalem's coming judgment through deportation. Phoenician cognates confirm the term's ancient Semitic usage for this specialized craft.

gloss_terse: heap, wave, billow (of water or grain)
gloss_readable: This noun appears in varied contexts denoting heaped masses—waves of the sea, piles of grain, or mounds of earth. Its semantic range extends from Exodus's heaped waters at the Red Sea crossing to Nehemiah's grain heaps and Jeremiah's burial mounds. The root conveys the basic image of something accumulated or piled high. When applied to water, it suggests waves or swells; for grain, threshing-floor piles; for tombs, earthen mounds. This metaphorical flexibility makes it useful across agricultural, geographical, and liturgical contexts.

senses.1: Heaps or piles appearing in multiple contexts: waves in Exodus 15:8, grain heaps in agricultural settings, or burial mounds. The word's flexibility allows it to describe anything heaped or accumulated. Multilingual evidence varies by context: 'waves' when describing water, 'heaps' for grain, 'mounds' for tombs. The unifying image is vertical accumulation, whether natural (waves) or human-made (threshing piles, burial cairns).

gloss_readable: This noun designates a rounded vessel or bowl, appearing in Ecclesiastes 12:6's enigmatic allegory of old age: 'before the silver cord is snapped, or the golden bowl is broken.' The word's root may relate to roundness or being bent into a circular shape. The metallic bowl in Ecclesiastes symbolizes life's fragility—precious yet breakable. Some lexical connections to spring or fountain sources suggest a possible relationship to water-holding vessels. The term's rarity (possibly unique in this form) contributes to Ecclesiastes' distinctive vocabulary.

senses.1: A rounded bowl or basin, specifically the 'golden bowl' in Ecclesiastes 12:6's allegory of death and aging. The precious metal emphasizes life's value, while breakability speaks to mortality. Translation evidence varies: some render generically as 'bowl,' others connect to spring/fountain imagery. The metaphorical context (paired with silver cord, wheel, pitcher) creates a network of fragile-yet-precious life symbols that shatter at death.

gloss_readable: This mountain range in northern Israel became infamous as the site of Saul's final battle and death. First and Second Samuel, along with Chronicles, repeatedly name Gilboa in connection with this catastrophic defeat by the Philistines. David's lament in 2 Samuel 1:21 curses the mountains: 'Let there be no dew or rain upon you, O mountains of Gilboa!' The name may mean 'bubbling spring' or relate to baldness/barrenness, ironically appropriate given David's curse. The geographical site remains identifiable in modern Israel, still bearing witness to that ancient tragedy.

senses.1: The mountain range where Saul and his sons died fighting the Philistines (1 Samuel 31; 2 Samuel 1). All languages preserve the proper name (Gilboa/Gilboa/Gilboa/Gilboa) through transliteration, standard for significant biblical geography. David's poetic curse made Gilboa synonymous with barrenness and tragedy in Israelite memory. The site's continued identification shows how certain biblical locations retain their names and associations across millennia.

gloss_readable: Multiple biblical locations bore this name, most famously the site near Jericho where Israel first camped after crossing Jordan and erected memorial stones. The name means 'circle' or 'wheel,' likely referring to stone circles at these sanctuary sites. Joshua 4-5 establishes Gilgal as Israel's first worship center in Canaan, where circumcision was renewed and Passover celebrated. Later texts mention a Gilgal in Benjamin's territory and possibly another in northern Israel. The prophets sometimes criticized Gilgal's corrupt worship. This name's popularity reflects the significance of circular stone monuments in ancient Israelite religion.

senses.1: A place name (primarily the Jordan valley site) meaning 'circle,' likely of memorial stones erected by Joshua (Joshua 4:19-20). All languages transliterate Gilgal unchanged, recognizing its status as a major biblical site. The etymology connects to the Hebrew root for 'roll,' which Joshua 5:9 exploits in a wordplay: 'I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt.' Multiple Gilgals in biblical geography reflect the name's association with sacred stone circles.

gloss_readable: This anatomical term appears primarily in violent contexts—battlefield deaths, executions, and Jael's famous tent-peg blow to Sisera's skull. The word specifically denotes the cranium or head bone rather than the head generally. Judges 9:53 describes a woman dropping a millstone on Abimelech's skull; 1 Chronicles 10:10 reports the Philistines fastening Saul's skull in the temple of Dagon. Most famously, 'Golgotha' derives from the Aramaic form meaning 'place of a skull.' The term's consistent association with death and violence made it apt for naming the crucifixion site.

senses.1: The skull or cranium in military and execution contexts. Judges, Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles use it when describing fatal head wounds or trophy-taking (enemy skulls displayed in temples). The Aramaic cognate gave rise to 'Golgotha' in the Gospels. Translations consistently render as 'skull' across languages, as the anatomical specificity (bone rather than flesh) matters for understanding the violent contexts—crushing blows, trophy displays, and the crucifixion site's name.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes skin or hide, appearing in contexts from human skin (Job's disease-ravaged flesh) to leather objects. Job 16:15 has the sufferer sewing sackcloth on his skin; Leviticus 13 uses related terms for skin diseases requiring priestly inspection. The word can also mean parchment or leather made from animal hides. The semantic range from living skin to processed leather reflects the material culture of ancient Israel, where animal hides provided writing surfaces, water containers, and clothing. The NIV's rendering varies by context: 'skin' for bodies, 'leather' for manufactured goods.

senses.1: Skin (human or animal) or leather made from hides. Job uses it for diseased human skin (16:15), while Leviticus employs related forms for dermatological diagnosis. When processed, the same word can mean leather or parchment for practical uses. Translations distinguish by context: bodily skin receives anatomical terms, while manufactured leather gets material-culture vocabulary. The Hebrew makes no such distinction, seeing continuity between living hide and processed material.

gloss_terse: to uncover, reveal, expose, go into exile
gloss_readable: This versatile verb encompasses uncovering physical objects (removing a cover), revealing secrets (disclosure), exposing nakedness (shameful or intimate), and going into exile (being carried away). The semantic unity lies in removing what conceals or confines. Genesis 9:21 has Noah uncovering himself in drunkenness; Ruth 3:4 involves uncovering feet in courtship ritual; numerous prophetic texts speak of Israel going into exile—'being uncovered' from their land. The term's range from mundane acts to covenant curses demonstrates Hebrew's preference for concrete verbs with broad metaphorical application.

senses.1: To uncover, remove a covering, or reveal what was hidden—physically (removing a roof, uncovering feet), informatively (revealing secrets), sexually (exposing nakedness), or geopolitically (exile as 'uncovering' a nation from its land). The verb's flexibility allows it to describe Ruth's modest courtship signal, Levitical prohibitions against sexual exposure, prophetic oracles about Babylonian exile, and God revealing mysteries. All share the core action of removing concealment or constraint.

gloss_readable: The noun form of 'uncover,' this term specifically denotes exile or captivity—the state of being removed from one's land. It appears frequently in prophetic literature announcing or describing the Babylonian deportation. Ezekiel uses it extensively; Amos speaks of Israel going 'into exile beyond Damascus.' The word captures exile's essence: Israel 'uncovered' or 'exposed,' stripped from the land that clothed their covenant identity. Later Jewish usage made it a technical term for diaspora existence, maintaining the image of displacement and exposure even centuries after the return.

senses.1: The condition of exile or captivity, especially the Babylonian deportation but also Assyrian and later dispersions. Prophetic texts employ it to warn of coming judgment (Amos 1:5) or lament its fulfillment (Lamentations). The root meaning 'uncovering' adds theological depth: exile strips away the land-covenant security, leaving Israel exposed among nations. Post-biblical Hebrew made it the standard term for diaspora existence, preserving the biblical metaphor.

gloss_readable: This town in Judah's hill country appears in Joshua 15:51's territorial list and gains tragic prominence as Ahithophel's hometown. Second Samuel 15:12 identifies Ahithophel as 'the Gilohite,' and his betrayal of David—joining Absalom's revolt—carries geographical irony since both he and David came from Judahite towns. The name may derive from roots meaning 'exile' or 'uncovering,' though such etymologies remain speculative. The site's exact location remains debated, though proposed identifications place it in the Hebron highlands near David's early power base.

senses.1: A town in Judah's hill country (Joshua 15:51), most notable as Ahithophel's hometown (2 Samuel 15:12). All languages preserve the proper name (Giloh/Guilo) through transliteration. The geographical detail gains narrative significance through the Ahithophel connection: David's trusted counselor who betrayed him came from David's own tribal territory, deepening the treachery. Archaeological identification remains uncertain despite proposals in the Hebron region.
